title: Chain stitch
subtitle: The foundation row and the spacer of crochet
excerpt: The chain is the simplest crochet stitch and the one almost everything is built on. A row of chains makes the foundation you work your first row into, and single chains worked mid-pattern open up the spaces in lace and granny work.
sourceNotes: Reconstructed in our own words from Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Chapter 9 (Crochet Work), the passage on the chain stitch and the position of the hands (Fig. 403). Public domain via Project Gutenberg. The chain stitch name is the same in UK and US terminology.

glossaryTerms.definition: The simplest crochet stitch, made by drawing the yarn through the loop on the hook. A row of chains is the usual foundation; single chains worked into a pattern make the open spaces in lace and granny work.
The starting row of chain stitches that the first row of a flat piece is worked into. Its length sets the width of the work.
The gap left under one or more chains worked over a stitch. Later rows work into the space rather than into the chain itself, which is how lace and granny patterns open up.

content.text: Begin with a slip knot on the hook and the working yarn tensioned over the fingers of your other hand.
Hold the slip knot steady between finger and thumb, just below the hook.
Wrap the yarn over the hook from back to front.
Draw the yarn through the loop already on the hook. One chain is made.
Repeat for each chain, sliding your grip up the work every few stitches to keep the tension even.
Count the V-shaped loops along the front to check the length. Do not count the loop sitting on the hook.

Every flat piece that does not start in the round begins with a foundation chain. Inside a pattern, chains make turning chains at the start of a row, corner and side spaces in motifs, and the open mesh of filet and lace. The chain is the most-used stitch in crochet, so getting an even, not-too-tight chain pays off in every project that follows.

A chainless or foundation-treble start works the first row of stitches and their base chain at the same time, giving a stretchier edge for garments. A picot is a tiny loop of three or four chains closed back on itself, used to trim edgings. Where a plain chain feels too tight to work into, going up one hook size for the foundation alone is the common fix.
Difficulty: beginner. The chain is usually the first stitch taught after the slip knot.
